title: Geotropism, Hydrotropism & Chemotropism (Pollen Tube Growth)
tagline: Gravity, moisture gradients, and chemical guidance of reproductive tissues.
theoryHtml:
Plants display a range of directional growth responses (tropisms) governed by different physical and chemical environmental signals:

1. Geotropism (Response to Gravity):

The directional growth of plant organs in response to the pull of gravity is called geotropism (or gravitropism):

  • Plant Roots: Grow downwards in the direction of the gravitational pull $\implies$ Positive Geotropism (anchors the plant securely in soil).
  • Plant Shoots (Stems): Grow upwards against the gravitational pull $\implies$ Negative Geotropism.

2. Hydrotropism (Response to Water):

The growth movement of plant roots towards moisture or water sources is called hydrotropism. Roots exhibit positive hydrotropism. In laboratory demonstrations where seeds are germinated near a porous clay cup filled with water, root tips curve sideways towards moisture, proving that hydrotropic attraction can even override geotropic pull!

3. Chemotropism (Response to Chemical Stimuli):

The directional growth movement of plant parts in response to specific chemical substances is called chemotropism:

  • Classic Example — Pollen Tube Growth: When a pollen grain lands on the compatible stigma of a flower during pollination, it germinates and develops a long pollen tube.
  • The pollen tube grows downward through the style towards the ovary and penetrates the ovule.
  • This directional growth is guided by chemical attractants (sugars and calcium gradients) secreted by the female ovule—a prime example of positive chemotropism!
pointsToRemember: Geotropism is growth in response to gravity: roots show positive geotropism; shoots show negative geotropism.
Hydrotropism is directional growth of roots towards moisture.
Chemotropism is directional growth guided by chemicals, exemplified by the growth of the pollen tube towards the ovule.
keyNotes: Board Classic: Give an example of chemotropism in plants: The growth of the pollen tube towards the ovule in response to chemical secretions.

questions.question: Why do plants wilt and shed leaves during severe prolonged drought?
options: Elevated levels of abscisic acid (ABA) close stomata to conserve water and trigger senescence and leaf abscission
questions.answer: Elevated levels of abscisic acid (ABA) close stomata to conserve water and trigger senescence and leaf abscission
questions.explanation: Water stress synthesizes ABA in roots and leaves, triggering guard cell potassium efflux (stomatal closure) and abscission zone development.

questions.question: What prevents the transmission of electrical nerve impulses from jumping uncontrollably between adjacent parallel axon fibres in a nerve bundle?
options: Insulating fatty myelin sheaths covering the axons
questions.answer: Insulating fatty myelin sheaths covering the axons
questions.explanation: Myelin sheaths produced by Schwann cells/oligodendrocytes provide electrical insulation, preventing cross-talk and enabling saltatory conduction.

questions.question: In the male reproductive system, which hormone is required both for developing secondary sexual traits and for stimulating the production of sperms?
questions.answer: Testosterone
questions.explanation: Testosterone acts locally on testicular seminiferous tubules to stimulate spermatogenesis and systemically to induce male virilization.

questions.question: Which of the following actions is a pure cranial reflex (integrated in the brainstem rather than the spinal cord)?
options: Blinking of eyes when an object approaches, and salivation at the sight of food
Withdrawing hand from a hot kettle
questions.answer: Blinking of eyes when an object approaches, and salivation at the sight of food
questions.explanation: Corneal blink and salivation reflexes are mediated through cranial nerves (trigeminal, facial, glossopharyngeal) via brainstem centres.

questions.question: Why do ripened fruits (like bananas or apples) accelerate the ripening of other unripened fruits kept nearby in the same basket?
options: Ripening fruits release the gaseous phytohormone ethylene, which diffuses through air to stimulate ripening enzymes in adjacent fruits
questions.answer: Ripening fruits release the gaseous phytohormone ethylene, which diffuses through air to stimulate ripening enzymes in adjacent fruits
questions.explanation: Ethylene (C₂H₄) is a volatile gaseous plant hormone that promotes fruit softening, starch conversion to sugars, and chlorophyll breakdown.

questions.question: Which of the following biological phenomena is the classic example of chemotropism in flowering plants?
options: Opening of flower petals at sunrise
Growth of the pollen tube through the style towards the ovule in response to chemical attractants
Bending of a shoot towards light
questions.answer: Growth of the pollen tube through the style towards the ovule in response to chemical attractants
questions.explanation: Chemical signals from the ovule guide the unidirectional growth of the pollen tube through the style.

questions.question: What type of tropism is displayed when plant roots grow downwards into the earth in the direction of gravitational pull?
questions.answer: Positive geotropism
questions.explanation: Growth towards the gravitational pull of the Earth is defined as positive geotropism.

questions.question: If a potted plant is placed horizontally on its side in a dark room, what growth curvature will be observed in its shoots and roots after a few days?
options: Both shoot and roots continue growing strictly horizontal.
The shoot bends upwards (negative geotropism) while roots bend downwards (positive geotropism).
The shoot bends downwards and roots grow upwards.
The plant stops all growth permanently.
questions.answer: The shoot bends upwards (negative geotropism) while roots bend downwards (positive geotropism).
questions.explanation: Gravity redistribution of auxin causes the shoot to curve upward and the root to curve downward.

questions.question: What directional response is termed 'hydrotropism' in botanical physiology?
options: Growth of plant parts in response to moisture and water gradients
Growth of leaves in dry air
questions.answer: Growth of plant parts in response to moisture and water gradients
questions.explanation: Hydrotropism is directional growth where moisture serves as the orienting environmental stimulus.

questions.question: Why does positive geotropism in roots offer an evolutionary survival advantage to land plants?
options: It exposes roots to bright sunlight.
It firmly anchors the plant in soil and brings roots into contact with subterranean water and mineral nutrients.
questions.answer: It firmly anchors the plant in soil and brings roots into contact with subterranean water and mineral nutrients.
questions.explanation: Downwards root growth ensures mechanical stability and access to soil moisture and inorganic minerals.

title: Thigmotropism & Tendril Coiling Around Supports
tagline: Touch-induced differential growth, mechanical anchoring, and climber adaptations.
theoryHtml:
Plants with weak, slender stems (such as climbing peas, bitter gourd, and grapevines) cannot stand upright on their own. To elevate their foliage towards sunlight, they produce specialized thread-like sensory organs called tendrils.

What Is Thigmotropism?

The directional growth response of a plant organ in reaction to physical contact or touch with a solid object is called thigmotropism. Tendrils exhibit positive thigmotropism.

The Cellular Mechanism of Tendril Coiling:

Tendrils are exquisitely sensitive to touch. How does a straight tendril wrap itself into a tight spiral around a fence or bamboo stake?

  1. Initial Contact: When a waving tendril brushes against a solid support, sensory mechanoreceptors detect the contact.
  2. Unequal Growth Rate (Differential Elongation):
    • The side of the tendril in direct physical contact with the support experiences a reduction in growth rate.
    • Auxin migrates away from the contact surface, accumulating on the side of the tendril away from the support.
    • This higher auxin concentration stimulates the outer, non-touching cells to grow and elongate significantly faster than the inner touching cells.
  3. Coiling and Anchoring: Because the outer side grows much faster than the inner side, the tendril bends tightly inwards around the support, forming a firm helical coil like a spring. This anchors the climbing plant securely and pulls the weak stem upward!
pointsToRemember: Thigmotropism is directional growth in response to physical contact or touch.
Tendrils of climbing plants (like peas) coil around supports via differential growth.
The side of the tendril in contact with the support grows slower, while the opposite side grows faster, causing the tendril to coil.
keyNotes: Exam Question: Explain how tendrils of a pea plant coil around a support (Side away from support grows faster than the side in contact, causing the tendril to circle and coil).

questions.question: In a laboratory experiment on action potential conduction, if a motor axon is treated with a neurotoxin that selectively blocks voltage-gated potassium (K⁺) channels, what will be the direct electrophysiological consequence?
options: Resting membrane potential becomes positive immediately
The neuron can depolarize, but repolarization back to the resting negative potential is severely prolonged/blocked, preventing generation of subsequent impulses
The axon conducts at the speed of light
questions.answer: The neuron can depolarize, but repolarization back to the resting negative potential is severely prolonged/blocked, preventing generation of subsequent impulses
questions.explanation: Voltage-gated K⁺ channels mediate outward repolarising current. Blocking them prevents rapid membrane repolarisation, maintaining prolonged refractory depolarization.

questions.question: Consider a patient presenting with elevated blood thyroxin (T4) levels, tachycardia, heat intolerance, weight loss despite increased appetite, and a low level of thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH). What is the underlying endocrine mechanism?
options: Primary hyperthyroidism (Graves' disease) where autonomous excess thyroxin exerts powerful negative feedback inhibition on the pituitary gland, suppressing TSH
questions.answer: Primary hyperthyroidism (Graves' disease) where autonomous excess thyroxin exerts powerful negative feedback inhibition on the pituitary gland, suppressing TSH
questions.explanation: In primary hyperthyroidism, autonomous overproduction of thyroxin by the thyroid gland triggers strong negative feedback at the anterior pituitary, suppressing TSH secretion.

questions.question: A plant seedling is grown inside a horizontally rotating clinostat (a device that rotates slowly around a horizontal axis at 1 rpm). What pattern of shoot and root growth will be observed?
options: Shoot bends upward, root bends downward
Both shoot and root continue to grow straight horizontally without curving, because continuous rotation equally distributes gravitational stimulus on all sides
questions.answer: Both shoot and root continue to grow straight horizontally without curving, because continuous rotation equally distributes gravitational stimulus on all sides
questions.explanation: A clinostat continuously rotates the plant, neutralizing the unidirectional gravity vector. Auxin is uniformly distributed on all sides, preventing geotropic curvature.

questions.question: In synaptic transmission, what is the precise biochemical sequence triggered when an action potential arrives at the presynaptic axon terminal?
options: Voltage-gated Ca²⁺ channels open $\rightarrow$ Ca²⁺ influx $\rightarrow$ Synaptic vesicle exocytosis $\rightarrow$ Neurotransmitter diffusion across cleft $\rightarrow$ Binding to ligand-gated postsynaptic receptors $\rightarrow$ Postsynaptic ion influx
K⁺ channels open $\rightarrow$ Vesicles dissolve in blood $\rightarrow$ Dendrite contracts
DNA is transcribed into neurotransmitters $\rightarrow$ Electrical spark across synapse
Myelin melts $\rightarrow$ Current jumps to next cell body
questions.answer: Voltage-gated Ca²⁺ channels open $\rightarrow$ Ca²⁺ influx $\rightarrow$ Synaptic vesicle exocytosis $\rightarrow$ Neurotransmitter diffusion across cleft $\rightarrow$ Binding to ligand-gated postsynaptic receptors $\rightarrow$ Postsynaptic ion influx
questions.explanation: Depolarization opens presynaptic Ca²⁺ channels. Calcium influx triggers SNARE-mediated fusion of acetylcholine vesicles, releasing transmitter to gate postsynaptic ionophores.

questions.question: Why does the removal of the apical bud (decapitation / pruning) in tea plantations and garden hedges promote dense, bushy lateral growth?
options: The apical bud produces high auxin concentrations that maintain 'apical dominance' by suppressing lateral axillary buds; removing the apex eliminates auxin inhibition, allowing cytokinins to stimulate lateral branching
Pruning causes the roots to grow into branches
questions.answer: The apical bud produces high auxin concentrations that maintain 'apical dominance' by suppressing lateral axillary buds; removing the apex eliminates auxin inhibition, allowing cytokinins to stimulate lateral branching
questions.explanation: Apical dominance is mediated by basipetal auxin flow from the shoot apex. Decapitation removes this apical auxin clamp, allowing endogenous cytokinins to activate dormant axillary buds.

questions.question: What botanical term describes the directional growth movement of a climbing plant's tendril in response to touch?
questions.answer: Thigmotropism
questions.explanation: Thigmotropism is the directional growth response stimulated by physical touch or contact.

questions.question: Why does a pea tendril coil tightly around a wooden bamboo stick when it touches it?
options: The side of the tendril in contact with the support grows slower, while the outer side away from the support grows much faster, forcing the tendril to coil.
The tendril melts and sticks to the wood.
questions.answer: The side of the tendril in contact with the support grows slower, while the outer side away from the support grows much faster, forcing the tendril to coil.
questions.explanation: Differential growth rates between contact and non-contact sides cause the helical coiling of tendrils.

questions.question: Which plant hormone is responsible for redistributing away from the contact point to stimulate elongation on the outer side of the tendril?
questions.answer: Auxin
questions.explanation: Auxin concentrates on the side away from contact, promoting localized cell elongation.

questions.question: Which of the following plants uses modified leaf or stem tendrils showing thigmotropism to climb supports?
questions.answer: Sweet pea (Pisum sativum)
questions.explanation: Pea plants possess delicate leaflet tendrils that coil around trellises via thigmotropism.

questions.question: What mechanical advantage does the coiled, spring-like structure of a tendril provide to a climbing plant during heavy winds?
options: It acts as a flexible shock absorber, holding the plant to its support without tearing the delicate stem.
It conducts electricity from the clouds.
questions.answer: It acts as a flexible shock absorber, holding the plant to its support without tearing the delicate stem.
questions.explanation: The helical coil acts like a mechanical spring, buffering wind gusts without ripping the climber.

title: Plant Hormones (Growth Promoters): Auxins, Gibberellins & Cytokinins
tagline: Endogenous chemical regulators stimulating cell division, elongation, and shoot development.
theoryHtml:
Plant coordination is accomplished entirely through chemical messengers called phytohormones (plant hormones). Unlike animal hormones, plant hormones are not produced in specialized glands; they are synthesized in tissues and diffuse readily to target cells. Plant hormones that stimulate growth are categorized as growth promoters:

1. Auxins:

  • Synthesized predominantly at the growing tips of shoots and roots.
  • Key Roles:
    • Promotes cell elongation and enlargement.
    • Coordinates phototropism (diffuses to shaded side to bend shoot towards light).
    • Maintains apical dominance (suppresses growth of lateral axillary buds).
    • Promotes root initiation in stem cuttings.

2. Gibberellins:

  • First discovered in rice seedlings infected with the 'foolish seedling' fungus Gibberella fujikuroi.
  • Key Roles:
    • Promotes stem elongation and inter-node growth, helping dwarf varieties grow tall.
    • Breaks seed dormancy and initiates seed germination by activating hydrolytic enzymes like alpha-amylase.
    • Promotes development of seedless fruits (parthenocarpy).

3. Cytokinins:

  • Hormones that specifically stimulate cell division (cytokinesis).
  • Key Roles:
    • Present in highest natural concentrations in areas of rapid cell division—namely young fruits, developing seeds, and root apices.
    • Promotes the opening of stomata even in darkness.
    • Delays leaf aging and yellowing (senescence) by preserving chlorophyll and cellular proteins.
pointsToRemember: Auxin promotes cell elongation and mediates phototropism and apical dominance.
Gibberellins promote stem growth, elongation of internodes, and seed germination.
Cytokinins promote rapid cell division and are present in high concentrations in fruits and seeds; delay leaf senescence.
keyNotes: Board Highlight: Name the plant hormone that promotes cell division (Cytokinins), and the hormone that helps in growth of stems (Gibberellins/Auxins).

questions.question: Which plant hormone, like auxin, promotes stem growth and elongation of internodes?
questions.answer: Gibberellins
questions.explanation: Gibberellins promote stem elongation, bolting, and breaking of seed dormancy.

questions.question: Which plant hormone is present in greatest concentration in areas of rapid cell division, such as developing fruits and seeds?
questions.answer: Cytokinins
questions.explanation: Cytokinins actively stimulate cytokinesis (cell division) and are abundant in actively proliferating tissues like root apices, developing seeds, and fruits.

questions.question: Which plant hormone acts as a growth inhibitor and induces wilting and abscission of leaves?
questions.answer: Abscisic acid (ABA)
questions.explanation: Abscisic acid (ABA) is a plant stress hormone that inhibits growth, causes stomatal closure during drought, and promotes leaf senescence and wilting.

questions.question: How do pea plant tendrils coil tightly around a physical support wire or bamboo stick (Thigmotropism)?
options: The side touching the support grows faster
Auxin diffuses away from the contact point; the part of the tendril away from the support grows much faster than the contact part, causing it to circle and cling
questions.answer: Auxin diffuses away from the contact point; the part of the tendril away from the support grows much faster than the contact part, causing it to circle and cling
questions.explanation: Contact with support inhibits cell elongation on the inner touching surface, while auxins stimulate rapid elongation on the outer side, coiling the tendril.

questions.question: Which emergency hormone is secreted directly into the blood by adrenal glands in scary or stress situations ('Fight or Flight' response)?
questions.answer: Adrenaline
questions.explanation: Adrenaline (epinephrine) from the adrenal medulla prepares the body for physical emergency by elevating heart rate, blood pressure, and skeletal muscle blood flow.

questions.question: Which plant hormone is specifically characterized by its ability to promote active cell division (cytokinesis) in plant tissues?
questions.answer: Cytokinins
questions.explanation: Cytokinins directly stimulate cytokinesis and cell division, found abundantly in dividing tissues.

questions.question: In which plant organs or structures are cytokinins naturally found in the highest physiological concentrations?
options: In areas of rapid cell division, such as developing fruits and seeds
questions.answer: In areas of rapid cell division, such as developing fruits and seeds
questions.explanation: Tissues undergoing intense cellular proliferation (embryos, seeds, young fruits) have high cytokinin levels.

questions.question: Which plant hormone, working alongside auxin, is primarily responsible for promoting stem elongation and inter-nodal growth in plants?
questions.answer: Gibberellin
questions.explanation: Gibberellins promote axial elongation of stem internodes and stimulate seed germination.

questions.question: Where is the plant growth hormone auxin primarily synthesized within a growing plant?
options: At the shoot and root apical meristematic tips
In the middle of mature woody bark
questions.answer: At the shoot and root apical meristematic tips
questions.explanation: Auxin is synthesized by dividing apical meristems at shoot and root tips and transported basipetally.

questions.question: Florists frequently spray cut flowers and leafy vegetables with dilute cytokinin solutions. What is the commercial purpose of this treatment?
options: To delay leaf senescence (aging and yellowing) and maintain fresh green appearance
questions.answer: To delay leaf senescence (aging and yellowing) and maintain fresh green appearance
questions.explanation: Cytokinins retard senescence and chlorophyll breakdown, prolonging post-harvest shelf life.

title: Plant Hormones (Growth Inhibitors): Abscisic Acid (ABA) & Ethylene
tagline: Dormancy induction, the drought stress hormone, and gaseous fruit ripening.
theoryHtml:
Just as an automobile requires brakes as well as an accelerator, plants require growth-inhibiting hormones to stop growth, conserve water, and survive hostile environmental conditions:

1. Abscisic Acid (ABA) — The Stress Hormone:

  • General Role: The master growth inhibitor in plants, counteracting the effects of growth-promoting hormones (auxins and gibberellins).
  • Drought Adaptation (The 'Stress Hormone'):
    • When roots detect soil moisture deficit (drought stress), they synthesize abscisic acid and transport it rapidly through xylem to leaves.
    • ABA signals guard cells to undergo rapid exosmosis, causing them to become flaccid and close stomatal pores immediately. This halts transpirational water loss, saving the plant from wilting.
  • Wilting & Abscission: Promotes the aging, yellowing, wilting, and dropping of leaves, flowers, and ripe fruits by forming an abscission layer across the petiole base.
  • Dormancy: Inhibits seed germination and induces dormancy in seeds and buds, ensuring seeds do not sprout during harsh freezing winters.

2. Ethylene ($\text{C}_2\text{H}_4$) — The Gaseous Ripening Hormone:

  • Ethylene is a natural hydrocarbon gas synthesized by ripening fruits and aging tissues.
  • Fruit Ripening: Accelerates the ripening of fruits (bananas, mangoes, tomatoes) by stimulating the conversion of complex insoluble starches into sweet soluble sugars, softening pectin cell walls, and synthesizing fruit aroma esters.
  • Commercial Practice: Green, unripe fruits are transported across long distances in refrigerated containers and subsequently exposed to controlled ethylene gas in ripening chambers before market retail.
pointsToRemember: Abscisic Acid (ABA) is the primary plant growth inhibitor.
ABA is the 'stress hormone' that closes stomata during drought and induces leaf wilting/falling (abscission).
Ethylene is the gaseous hormone that promotes commercial and natural fruit ripening.
keyNotes: Board Highlight: Name the plant hormone responsible for wilting of leaves (Abscisic Acid, ABA).

questions.question: A neurosurgeon testing cortical localization stimulates a specific region on the precentral gyrus of the left cerebral cortex during awake brain surgery. What motor response will be elicited in the patient?
options: Involuntary pupil constriction in left eye
Contraction of voluntary skeletal muscles on the contralateral (right) side of the patient's body
Sudden secretion of insulin from pancreas
Complete loss of hearing in left ear
questions.answer: Contraction of voluntary skeletal muscles on the contralateral (right) side of the patient's body
questions.explanation: The primary motor cortex on the precentral gyrus maps motor outputs that decussate (cross over) in the medullary pyramids, controlling contralateral voluntary musculature.

questions.question: In a patient with Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus, autoimmune destruction of which specific cell population in the pancreas leads to an absolute inability to synthesize insulin?
options: Beta cells ($\beta$-cells) of the islets of Langerhans
questions.answer: Beta cells ($\beta$-cells) of the islets of Langerhans
questions.explanation: Type 1 Diabetes involves cell-mediated autoimmune destruction of pancreatic beta cells, abolishing proinsulin synthesis.

questions.question: What is the physiological basis of 'saltatory conduction' along myelinated nerve fibres compared to continuous unmyelinated conduction?
options: Myelin conducts electricity like copper wire
Myelin sheaths insulate the axon except at Nodes of Ranvier, forcing action potentials to jump from node to node, vastly increasing conduction velocity up to 120 m/s with minimal energy expenditure
Salt crystals in myelin create sparks
Myelinated fibres do not use sodium ions
questions.answer: Myelin sheaths insulate the axon except at Nodes of Ranvier, forcing action potentials to jump from node to node, vastly increasing conduction velocity up to 120 m/s with minimal energy expenditure
questions.explanation: Myelin provides high transmembrane resistance and low capacitance. Voltage-gated Na⁺ channels clustered at Ranvier nodes allow depolarizing currents to jump electrotonically between nodes.

questions.question: Consider an experimental seedling exposed to unilateral blue light (450 nm) versus red light (660 nm). Why does phototropic bending occur vigorously under blue light but negligibly under red light?
options: Phototropin photoreceptors at the shoot tip specifically absorb blue light wavelengths to trigger asymmetric lateral auxin phosphorylation and translocation
Red light destroys all plant cells
questions.answer: Phototropin photoreceptors at the shoot tip specifically absorb blue light wavelengths to trigger asymmetric lateral auxin phosphorylation and translocation
questions.explanation: Phototropins (phot1/phot2) are blue-light flavoprotein photoreceptors whose kinase activation establishes the lateral auxin concentration gradient driving phototropism.

questions.question: How does the hypothalamus-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis differ functionally from the immediate sympathetic-adrenal medullary (SAM) pathway during severe prolonged stress?
options: SAM provides immediate neural-adrenaline fight-or-flight within seconds, while HPA releases CRH $\rightarrow$ ACTH $\rightarrow$ Cortisol over hours to sustain gluconeogenesis and stress adaptation
HPA works in milliseconds; SAM takes days
Both systems secrete identical amounts of insulin
questions.answer: SAM provides immediate neural-adrenaline fight-or-flight within seconds, while HPA releases CRH $\rightarrow$ ACTH $\rightarrow$ Cortisol over hours to sustain gluconeogenesis and stress adaptation
questions.explanation: The SAM axis provides instantaneous catecholamine surge via sympathetic splanchnic nerves. The HPA axis provides sustained hormonal glucocorticoid release (cortisol) to mobilize energy stores.

questions.question: Which plant hormone acts as a growth inhibitor and is directly responsible for the wilting and falling (abscission) of leaves?
questions.answer: Abscisic Acid (ABA)
questions.explanation: Abscisic acid (ABA) is an inhibitory hormone that induces leaf yellowing, wilting, and abscission.

questions.question: Why is Abscisic Acid (ABA) designated as the 'stress hormone' in plant physiology?
options: It causes plants to produce flowers during thunderstorms.
Under drought stress, ABA triggers the rapid closure of stomata to prevent fatal transpirational water loss.
It turns chlorophyll into red pigment.
questions.answer: Under drought stress, ABA triggers the rapid closure of stomata to prevent fatal transpirational water loss.
questions.explanation: ABA levels surge under osmotic stress, signalling guard cells to close stomata and conserve moisture.

questions.question: Which unique plant hormone exists as a gaseous hydrocarbon at ambient room temperatures and promotes fruit ripening?
questions.answer: Ethylene (C2H4)
questions.explanation: Ethylene is the only gaseous phytohormone, orchestrating fruit ripening and tissue senescence.

questions.question: How does Abscisic Acid (ABA) help seeds survive freezing winter conditions?
options: By maintaining seed dormancy and preventing premature germination until favorable spring conditions arrive
By turning the seed into a bulb
questions.answer: By maintaining seed dormancy and preventing premature germination until favorable spring conditions arrive
questions.explanation: ABA maintains developmental arrest (dormancy) so seeds survive unfavorable winter environments.

questions.question: Which of the following pairs correctly matches the phytohormone with its primary physiological function?
options: Abscisic acid — Closes stomata and inhibits growth
questions.answer: Abscisic acid — Closes stomata and inhibits growth
questions.explanation: ABA is an inhibitor that induces stomatal closure and retards vegetative growth.

title: Hormones in Animals: Electrical vs Chemical Signaling
tagline: Endocrine system principles, ductless glands, and universal cellular coordination.
theoryHtml:
Animals possess a highly sophisticated, high-speed nervous system. Why, then, did nature evolve a parallel endocrine system producing chemical hormones?

Limitations of Electrical Nerve Signaling:

  1. Incomplete Innervation: Electrical impulses can only reach those individual cells that are physically connected by nerve fibers. Millions of cells in the human body have no direct nerve connections!
  2. Refractory Reset Period: When a neuron generates and transmits an electrical action potential, it takes a finite amount of time (refractory period) to reset its cell membrane ionic gradients before it can fire a second impulse. Neurons cannot transmit continuous, unbroken signals.
  3. Localized Action: Nerve impulses are localized point-to-point signals unsuitable for orchestrating widespread, body-wide developmental changes.

The Endocrine Alternative — Chemical Hormonal Signaling:

  • Ductless Glands: Endocrine glands have no tubes or ducts; they secrete their chemical messengers (hormones) directly into the circulating bloodstream.
  • Universal Cellular Reach: The bloodstream circulates everywhere, carrying hormones to every single tissue and organ in the body.
  • Target Specificity: Although a hormone bathes all cells, it acts ONLY upon specific target cells possessing complementary surface receptor proteins.
  • Sustained & Coordinated Responses: Hormones produce steady, coordinated, and long-lasting biological responses, making them ideal for governing body-wide transitions such as growth, metabolic rates, and sexual maturity at puberty.
pointsToRemember: Electrical impulses reach only innervated cells and require refractory time to reset.
Endocrine glands are ductless and secrete hormones directly into the bloodstream.
Hormones travel everywhere in blood, acting specifically on target cells possessing complementary receptors.
Chemical coordination is steady, prolonged, and ideal for body-wide growth and development.
keyNotes: Core Reasoning Question: Why is chemical signaling (hormones) necessary in animals despite having a nervous system? (Nerves do not reach all cells, and cells need time to reset after impulses; hormones reach everywhere via blood).

questions.question: What physiological changes occur in the body when adrenaline is released into the bloodstream?
options: Heart rate slows down and breathing stops
Heart beats faster, breathing rate increases, and blood is diverted from skin/digestive tract to skeletal muscles
questions.answer: Heart beats faster, breathing rate increases, and blood is diverted from skin/digestive tract to skeletal muscles
questions.explanation: Adrenaline accelerates cardiac output, contracts smooth muscles around visceral arterioles (diverting blood to skeletal muscles), and increases ventilation rate.

questions.question: Which mineral element is essential for the thyroid gland to synthesize thyroxin hormone?
questions.answer: Iodine
questions.explanation: Iodine is a vital inorganic constituent of thyroxin (tetraiodothyronine / T4) produced by the thyroid gland.

questions.question: Deficiency of dietary iodine in humans causes enlargement of the thyroid gland, leading to the clinical condition called:
questions.answer: Goitre (Swollen neck)
questions.explanation: Iodine deficiency prevents thyroxin synthesis, prompting pituitary TSH hypersecretion and compensatory hypertrophy of the thyroid gland (endemic goitre).

questions.question: What is the primary physiological function of thyroxin hormone secreted by the thyroid gland?
options: Regulates carbohydrate, protein, and fat basal metabolism to provide the optimal balance for growth
questions.answer: Regulates carbohydrate, protein, and fat basal metabolism to provide the optimal balance for growth
questions.explanation: Thyroxin sets the basal metabolic rate (BMR), regulating cellular respiration, tissue differentiation, and nutrient metabolism.

questions.question: Growth hormone (GH) is secreted by which endocrine gland located at the base of the brain?
questions.answer: Pituitary gland
questions.explanation: The anterior pituitary gland secretes Growth Hormone (somatotropin), which stimulates cellular hypertrophy, mitotic division, and skeletal growth.

questions.question: What is the primary anatomical limitation of the nervous system that necessitates chemical hormonal coordination?
options: Electrical impulses can only reach cells connected by nerve fibers, whereas hormones reach all body tissues via the bloodstream.
The brain turns off after noon.
questions.answer: Electrical impulses can only reach cells connected by nerve fibers, whereas hormones reach all body tissues via the bloodstream.
questions.explanation: Not all cells are innervated; systemic blood circulation delivers endocrine signals to all cells.

questions.question: Why are endocrine glands medically classified as 'ductless glands'?
options: They lack tubes or ducts, secreting their chemical hormones directly into the circulating bloodstream.
questions.answer: They lack tubes or ducts, secreting their chemical hormones directly into the circulating bloodstream.
questions.explanation: Unlike exocrine glands (with ducts like salivary glands), endocrine glands release hormones directly into blood capillaries.

questions.question: After a neuron fires an electrical nerve impulse, why can it not immediately fire another impulse without a brief delay?
options: The neuron must wait for the brain to sleep.
The cell membrane must restore its resting ionic concentration gradients (the refractory period).
The neuron runs out of blood.
questions.answer: The cell membrane must restore its resting ionic concentration gradients (the refractory period).
questions.explanation: The sodium-potassium ATPase pump requires a refractory recovery interval to reset membrane potentials.

questions.question: Although a hormone circulates through all blood vessels across the entire body, why does it affect ONLY specific target organs?
options: The hormone is destroyed by red blood cells.
Only target cells possess specific complementary molecular receptor proteins that bind that particular hormone.
The hormone is guided by magnetic fields.
questions.answer: Only target cells possess specific complementary molecular receptor proteins that bind that particular hormone.
questions.explanation: Target tissue selectivity is governed by specific hormone receptors expressed on or within target cells.

questions.question: Which of the following biological transitions is coordinated primarily by the endocrine system rather than the nervous system?
options: Jerking hand away from an open flame
Blinking of eyelids when an object approaches
Gradual development of secondary sexual characteristics during puberty
questions.answer: Gradual development of secondary sexual characteristics during puberty
questions.explanation: Pubertal maturation is a systemic, prolonged developmental transition orchestrated by endocrine gonadal steroids.

title: The Adrenal Glands: Adrenaline & The Fight-or-Flight Response
tagline: Emergency sympathetic activation, vascular redistribution, and survival physiology.
theoryHtml:
When an animal faces acute physical danger—such as an impala spotting a hunting cheetah, or a human encountering a fierce barking dog—its body must prepare instantly for survival. It must decide whether to fight the threat or flee at maximum speed. This full-body survival mobilisation is orchestrated by the hormone Adrenaline.

The Adrenal Glands:

Humans possess two adrenal glands, each positioned like a small cap directly on top of each kidney (suprarenal glands).

Physiological Cascade Triggered by Adrenaline:

Under fear, acute stress, or sudden physical danger, adrenaline is secreted directly into the bloodstream, triggering coordinated physiological adjustments:

  1. Accelerated Heartbeat: Adrenaline acts on the heart, causing it to beat faster and pump with greater force. This floods skeletal muscles with rich supplies of oxygen and glucose.
  2. Vascular Shunting (Redistribution of Blood):
    Blood flow to non-essential organs (the digestive gut and skin) is dramatically reduced by the constriction of small arteries around these tissues. This shunts massive volumes of oxygenated blood directly towards skeletal muscles in the limbs.
  3. Accelerated Breathing Rate: The respiratory rate increases rapidly due to contractions of the diaphragm and rib intercostal muscles, and bronchial air passages dilate to maximize oxygen uptake into the blood.
  4. Hepatic Glycogenolysis: The liver breaks down stored glycogen, flooding the bloodstream with glucose for immediate cellular ATP generation.

Together, these integrated responses prime the muscular apparatus of the animal to execute intense physical exertion (fight or flight) without immediate fatigue!
pointsToRemember: Adrenal glands (located atop the kidneys) secrete Adrenaline during emergency situations.
Adrenaline prepares the body for 'Fight or Flight' by increasing heart rate, breathing rate, and blood pressure.
Blood is diverted away from the digestive tract and skin toward skeletal muscles to support rapid physical action.
keyNotes: Board Highlight: State three physiological changes that occur when adrenaline is secreted into the blood: 1) Heart beats faster, 2) Breathing rate increases, 3) Blood is diverted from digestive tract/skin to skeletal muscles.

questions.question: Deficiency of growth hormone during childhood leads to which medical condition?
questions.answer: Pituitary Dwarfism
questions.explanation: Hyposecretion of GH in prepubertal children impairs bone and tissue elongation, causing proportionate dwarfism.

questions.question: Hypersecretion (excessive secretion) of growth hormone during childhood leads to:
questions.answer: Gigantism
questions.explanation: Excessive pituitary GH secretion before epiphyseal plate fusion results in abnormal vertical skeletal overgrowth (gigantism).

questions.question: Which male sex hormone secreted by the testes is responsible for the physical changes associated with puberty in boys?
questions.answer: Testosterone
questions.explanation: Testosterone produced by testicular Leydig cells stimulates secondary male sexual characteristics (deepening of voice, facial hair, muscular build) and spermatogenesis.

questions.question: Which female sex hormone secreted by ovaries is responsible for secondary sexual characteristics and menstrual cycle regulation in girls?
questions.answer: Oestrogen and Progesterone
questions.explanation: Oestrogen controls female secondary sexual traits and uterine proliferation; progesterone prepares and maintains the uterine endometrium for pregnancy.

questions.question: Which hormone is produced by beta cells of the islets of Langerhans in the pancreas to lower and regulate blood sugar levels?
questions.answer: Insulin
questions.explanation: Insulin facilitates cellular uptake and storage of glucose as glycogen in liver and muscle cells, lowering blood glucose concentration.

questions.question: Where are the adrenal glands anatomically situated in the human body?
options: In the base of the skull
Positioned like caps on top of both kidneys
Around the trachea in the neck
questions.answer: Positioned like caps on top of both kidneys
questions.explanation: The paired suprarenal adrenal glands sit atop the superior poles of both kidneys.

questions.question: What happens to the blood flow to the digestive digestive tract and skin when adrenaline is released during an acute emergency?
options: Blood flow to the gut and skin increases tenfold.
Blood flow to the digestive system and skin is drastically reduced, diverting blood towards skeletal muscles.
questions.answer: Blood flow to the digestive system and skin is drastically reduced, diverting blood towards skeletal muscles.
questions.explanation: Arteriolar vasoconstriction shunts blood from visceral organs to skeletal muscles to power fight-or-flight.

questions.question: Why does the human breathing rate accelerate rapidly following a sudden adrenaline surge?
options: To increase blood oxygenation by dilating bronchioles and stimulating diaphragm/rib contractions
To excrete urea through the mouth
questions.answer: To increase blood oxygenation by dilating bronchioles and stimulating diaphragm/rib contractions
questions.explanation: Adrenaline stimulates respiratory centers and dilates bronchioles, maximizing oxygen delivery.

questions.question: Which organ is stimulated by adrenaline to break down stored glycogen into glucose to fuel active muscles?
questions.answer: Liver
questions.explanation: Adrenaline promotes hepatic glycogenolysis, elevating blood glucose levels for muscle ATP production.

questions.question: Which of the following hormones is commonly termed the 'emergency hormone' or 'fight-or-flight hormone'?
questions.answer: Adrenaline (Epinephrine)
questions.explanation: Adrenaline prepares physiological systems for immediate emergency action (fight or flight).

title: The Thyroid Gland: Thyroxin, Iodine Requirement & Goitre
tagline: Basal metabolic rate regulation, dietary iodine trace needs, and preventing neck swellings.
theoryHtml:
1. The Thyroid Gland and Thyroxin:

The Thyroid Gland is a butterfly-shaped endocrine organ situated in the neck, wrapped around the front of the trachea (windpipe) just below the larynx. It synthesizes and secretes the hormone Thyroxin:

  • Function of Thyroxin: Thyroxin regulates the metabolism of carbohydrates, fats, and proteins in the body. By governing the rate at which cells consume oxygen and burn fuels, it controls the Basal Metabolic Rate (BMR), ensuring the optimal balance for physical growth and tissue development.

2. The Indispensable Role of Iodine:

Iodine is chemically essential for the synthesis of thyroxin. The thyroid gland cannot manufacture thyroxin molecules without incorporating dietary iodine atoms.

3. Iodine Deficiency and Goitre:

  • Pathology: In regions where soil and drinking water lack iodine (notably in mountainous and sub-Himalayan inland areas), people consume diets deficient in iodine.
  • When the thyroid gland cannot synthesize enough thyroxin, the pituitary gland continuously releases thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) to force the thyroid to work harder.
  • In response, the thyroid follicular cells proliferate massively, causing the entire thyroid gland to enlarge into a prominent swelling in the neck called Goitre.
  • Prevention: Goitre is easily and universally prevented by consuming iodised table salt ($NaCl$ fortified with trace amounts of potassium iodate, $\text{KIO}_3$), providing the tiny daily requirement ($150\ \mu\text{g}$) of iodine.
pointsToRemember: Thyroid gland in the neck secretes Thyroxin, which regulates carbohydrate, protein, and fat metabolism.
Iodine is essential for the synthesis of thyroxin in the thyroid gland.
Deficiency of iodine in the diet leads to enlargement of the thyroid gland, causing Goitre (swollen neck).
Iodised salt is recommended to prevent goitre.
keyNotes: Board Question Classic: Why is the use of iodised salt advised? (Iodine is essential for thyroid gland to make thyroxin; lack of iodine causes goitre with a swollen neck).

questions.question: A chronic deficiency or malfunction of insulin hormone causes high blood glucose and glucose in urine, a condition known as:
questions.answer: Diabetes mellitus
questions.explanation: Insulin insufficiency prevents glucose utilization, causing hyperglycemia and glucosuria (Diabetes mellitus).

questions.question: The precise timing and quantity of hormone release in the human body is regulated by an automatic regulatory system called a:
questions.answer: Feedback mechanism
questions.explanation: Negative feedback mechanisms adjust endocrine secretion: rising blood glucose triggers insulin release; as glucose drops, insulin output is down-regulated.

questions.question: Which part of the brain secretes releasing hormones (like Growth Hormone Releasing Factor) that stimulate the pituitary gland?
questions.answer: Hypothalamus
questions.explanation: The hypothalamus synthesizes neurohormonal releasing and inhibiting factors that regulate anterior pituitary gland secretions.

questions.question: Which of the following is a plant growth inhibitor?
questions.answer: Abscisic acid
questions.explanation: Abscisic acid (ABA) is a phytohormone that inhibits growth, induces dormancy, and promotes leaf abscission.

questions.question: Which part of the neuron transmits impulses AWAY from the cell body toward a synapse or effector muscle?
questions.answer: Axon
questions.explanation: The axon is the single long cylindrical cytoplasmic extension conducting impulses away from the cyton to the synapse.

questions.question: Why is the mandatory consumption of iodised table salt universally recommended by public health authorities?
options: Iodine makes table salt taste sweeter.
Iodine is chemically essential for the thyroid gland to synthesize thyroxin, preventing goitre.
Iodine turns salt into a powerful antibiotic.
questions.answer: Iodine is chemically essential for the thyroid gland to synthesize thyroxin, preventing goitre.
questions.explanation: Iodine is a necessary cofactor for thyroxin synthesis; deficiency causes thyroid hypertrophy (goitre).

questions.question: What is the characteristic visible clinical symptom of goitre caused by dietary iodine deficiency?
options: A dramatically swollen and enlarged neck
questions.answer: A dramatically swollen and enlarged neck
questions.explanation: Compensatory hypertrophy of the thyroid gland produces a visible cervical neck swelling.

questions.question: What is the primary physiological function of the hormone thyroxin secreted by the thyroid gland?
options: It regulates the metabolism of carbohydrates, fats, and proteins for optimal growth and basal metabolic rate (BMR).
It digests milk proteins in the stomach.
questions.answer: It regulates the metabolism of carbohydrates, fats, and proteins for optimal growth and basal metabolic rate (BMR).
questions.explanation: Thyroxin controls cellular metabolic rate, regulating oxygen consumption and heat production.

questions.question: In which geographical regions is dietary iodine deficiency and endemic goitre historically most prevalent?
options: Mountainous inland regions (such as the Himalayas) where rainwater has leached iodine from soil
questions.answer: Mountainous inland regions (such as the Himalayas) where rainwater has leached iodine from soil
questions.explanation: Glacial leaching strips iodine from mountain soils and waters, causing endemic goitre in local populations.

questions.question: Where is the thyroid gland anatomically situated in the human body?
options: At the base of the brain
In the neck region, attached to the front of the trachea
questions.answer: In the neck region, attached to the front of the trachea
questions.explanation: The bi-lobed thyroid gland wraps around the anterior and lateral surfaces of the trachea.

title: The Pituitary Gland: Growth Hormone, Dwarfism & Gigantism
tagline: The master endocrine gland, somatotropin regulation, and stature disorders.
theoryHtml:
1. The Pituitary Gland — The 'Master Gland':

The Pituitary Gland is a small, pea-sized endocrine organ situated at the base of the brain, suspended directly from the hypothalamus. It is traditionally designated the 'master gland' of the endocrine system because its trophic hormones control and regulate the secretions of other endocrine glands (including the thyroid, adrenal cortex, and gonads).

2. Growth Hormone (GH / Somatotropin):

One of the vital hormones secreted by the anterior pituitary is Growth Hormone:

  • Function: Regulates the growth, cellular division, and development of all tissues in the body, stimulating the elongation of long bones (femur, tibia, humerus) and skeletal muscles during childhood and adolescence.

3. Clinical Disorders of Growth Hormone Secretion:

  • Dwarfism (Hyposecretion in Childhood):
    • Caused by a deficiency (hyposecretion) of growth hormone during childhood.
    • The epiphyseal growth plates of long bones close prematurely.
    • The individual remains abnormally short in stature, but body proportions and mental intelligence remain normal.
  • Gigantism (Hypersecretion in Childhood):
    • Caused by excessive secretion (hypersecretion) of growth hormone during childhood (often due to a benign pituitary tumour).
    • Long bones grow to extraordinary lengths before the growth plates fuse.
    • The individual attains an abnormally immense height (frequently exceeding $2.1 - 2.4\text{ metres}$ or $7 - 8\text{ feet}$!).
pointsToRemember: The pituitary gland (master gland) at the base of the brain secretes Growth Hormone (GH).
Growth hormone regulates the growth and development of bones and tissues.
Deficiency of GH in childhood causes Dwarfism (very short stature); excess GH causes Gigantism (abnormally tall stature).
keyNotes: Board Highlight: State the consequence of: 1) Deficiency of growth hormone in childhood (Dwarfism), 2) Excessive secretion of growth hormone in childhood (Gigantism).

questions.question: Why does the administration of iodised table salt prevent goitre in populations living in mountainous or sub-Himalayan regions?
options: Mountain soils are leached of iodine by glacial runoff, resulting in iodine-deficient local crops; iodised salt supplies the dietary iodine required for thyroxin synthesis
questions.answer: Mountain soils are leached of iodine by glacial runoff, resulting in iodine-deficient local crops; iodised salt supplies the dietary iodine required for thyroxin synthesis
questions.explanation: Soils in mountainous regions lack iodine. Consuming potassium iodate/iodide-fortified salt prevents thyroid hypertrophy and endemic goitre.

questions.question: When a person accidentally steps on a sharp thorn, they instantly pull their foot away and then shout in pain. What explains this sequence of events?
options: The spinal reflex arc executes immediate muscular withdrawal in milliseconds, while collateral sensory neurons simultaneously transmit pain impulses up the spinal cord to the cerebral cortex for conscious perception and vocalization
Foot muscles have their own brain
questions.answer: The spinal reflex arc executes immediate muscular withdrawal in milliseconds, while collateral sensory neurons simultaneously transmit pain impulses up the spinal cord to the cerebral cortex for conscious perception and vocalization
questions.explanation: The local polysynaptic spinal reflex completes withdrawal before ascending spinothalamic tracts reach the somatosensory cortex for conscious pain awareness.

questions.question: Which of the following statements regarding plant hormones (phytohormones) is INCORRECT?
options: Cytokinins inhibit cell division and cause premature leaf fall
Abscisic acid promotes dormancy and stomatal closure
questions.answer: Cytokinins inhibit cell division and cause premature leaf fall
questions.explanation: Statement C is false. Cytokinins PROMOTE cell division and delay leaf senescence; Abscisic acid promotes leaf fall.

questions.question: In the human endocrine system, which gland is responsible for regulating blood calcium and phosphate levels?
questions.answer: Parathyroid glands (secreting Parathormone)
questions.explanation: Parathyroid glands secrete parathormone (PTH), which elevates serum calcium by stimulating bone resorption and renal calcium reabsorption.

questions.question: Why do auxins cause tendrils of climbing plants (like peas) to circle around a bamboo stake upon contact?
options: Mechanical touch triggers rapid migration of auxin to the non-contact side, accelerating outer cellular elongation relative to the inner touching side
questions.answer: Mechanical touch triggers rapid migration of auxin to the non-contact side, accelerating outer cellular elongation relative to the inner touching side
questions.explanation: Thigmotropic touch signals cause basipetal/lateral auxin translocation to the outer flank, promoting asymmetric differential growth.

questions.question: Which endocrine gland located at the base of the brain secretes Growth Hormone to regulate developmental stature?
questions.answer: Pituitary gland
questions.explanation: The anterior lobe of the pituitary gland synthesizes and releases Growth Hormone (somatotropin).

questions.question: What clinical medical condition results from a severe deficiency of Growth Hormone during childhood?
questions.answer: Dwarfism (extremely stunted physical stature)
questions.explanation: Childhood hyposecretion of growth hormone impairs bone elongation, causing pituitary dwarfism.

questions.question: What clinical condition is caused by an abnormal hypersecretion (excess) of Growth Hormone during early childhood before epiphyseal plates fuse?
questions.answer: Gigantism (abnormally tall vertical height)
questions.explanation: Childhood hypersecretion of GH stimulates excessive long-bone elongation, causing gigantism.

questions.question: Why is the pituitary gland traditionally referred to as the 'master gland' of the endocrine system?
options: It is the largest gland in the body.
It secretes trophic hormones that regulate and stimulate the activity of many other endocrine glands (thyroid, adrenals, gonads).
It filters blood before the heart.
questions.answer: It secretes trophic hormones that regulate and stimulate the activity of many other endocrine glands (thyroid, adrenals, gonads).
questions.explanation: Pituitary trophic hormones (TSH, ACTH, FSH, LH) control the secretory output of secondary target glands.

questions.question: Which neuroendocrine structure in the brain directly controls the release of pituitary hormones via releasing and inhibiting factors?
questions.answer: Hypothalamus
questions.explanation: The hypothalamus secretes releasing hormones (e.g. GHRH) that instruct the pituitary gland.

title: The Pancreas: Insulin, Blood Glucose Regulation & Diabetes Mellitus
tagline: Islets of Langerhans beta cells, glucose uptake, and daily insulin therapeutics.
theoryHtml:
1. The Pancreas — A Heterocrine (Dual) Gland:

The Pancreas is located in the abdominal cavity just behind the stomach. It is a dual organ possessing both exocrine functions (secreting pancreatic digestive juice via the pancreatic duct) and endocrine functions (secreting hormones directly into blood).

2. The Endocrine Secretion — Insulin:

  • Specialized micro-organs embedded within pancreatic tissue, called the Islets of Langerhans, contain beta ($\beta$) cells that synthesize and secrete the protein hormone Insulin.
  • Function of Insulin: Insulin acts as the master regulator that lowers blood glucose levels:
    1. Stimulates body cells (especially skeletal muscles and adipose tissue) to absorb glucose from circulating blood.
    2. Stimulates the liver and muscles to convert excess glucose into glycogen (glycogenesis).

3. Diabetes Mellitus:

  • Cause: When the pancreas fails to secrete adequate amounts of insulin, or when body cells become resistant to insulin, glucose cannot enter cells and remains trapped in the bloodstream.
  • Pathology: Blood sugar rises to dangerously high levels (hyperglycaemia). The kidneys filter out excess glucose, causing glucose to appear in the urine.
  • Symptoms: Extreme thirst (polydipsia), frequent urination (polyuria), weight loss, and chronic fatigue.
  • Management: Patients with severe diabetes (Type 1) are treated by regular, daily injections of insulin.

    Why must insulin be injected rather than swallowed as a pill? Insulin is a protein. If taken orally, stomach pepsin and pancreatic enzymes would digest insulin into harmless amino acids before it could enter the bloodstream!
pointsToRemember: Pancreatic Islets of Langerhans secrete the hormone Insulin.
Insulin lowers blood glucose levels by promoting cellular glucose uptake and glycogen storage.
Deficiency of insulin causes Diabetes mellitus (high blood sugar), treated by insulin injections.
Insulin must be injected because being a protein, it would be digested in the gut if swallowed.
keyNotes: Board Highlight: Name the hormone that regulates blood sugar levels (Insulin, secreted by the pancreas). Explain why diabetic patients are treated with insulin injections.

questions.question: What is the primary function of the hormone melatonin secreted by the pineal gland?
options: Regulates 24-hour diurnal biological rhythms (sleep-wake cycle) and body temperature
questions.answer: Regulates 24-hour diurnal biological rhythms (sleep-wake cycle) and body temperature
questions.explanation: Melatonin produced by the pineal gland regulates circadian sleep-wake cycles, pigmentation, and seasonal biological clocks.

questions.question: What happens when a potted plant is placed horizontally in a dark box illuminated ONLY from a small pinhole at the bottom?
options: Shoot bends downward towards the light source (positive phototropism overriding negative geotropism)
questions.answer: Shoot bends downward towards the light source (positive phototropism overriding negative geotropism)
questions.explanation: Phototropic response to directional illumination is strong and can reorient shoot growth toward the light vector even if it directs growth downward.

questions.question: Which of the following is a symptom of hypothyroidism in infants (Cretinism)?
options: Stunted physical growth and severe mental/cognitive impairment
questions.answer: Stunted physical growth and severe mental/cognitive impairment
questions.explanation: Congenital thyroid deficiency in infancy impairs neurogenesis and skeletal development, resulting in cretinism.

questions.question: Which division of the autonomic nervous system is responsible for 'Rest and Digest' activities (slowing heart rate, stimulating salivation and digestion)?
questions.answer: Parasympathetic nervous system
questions.explanation: The parasympathetic system conserves energy, slowing cardiac rate and promoting gastrointestinal peristalsis and secretion.

questions.question: What is the primary role of the thymus gland in the human body?
options: Secretes thymosin, which aids in the maturation and differentiation of T-lymphocytes for cell-mediated immunity
questions.answer: Secretes thymosin, which aids in the maturation and differentiation of T-lymphocytes for cell-mediated immunity
questions.explanation: The thymus produces thymosin peptide hormones essential for T-cell immunocompetence during early life.

questions.question: Which hormone produced by the beta cells of the pancreas is responsible for lowering and regulating blood glucose levels?
questions.answer: Insulin
questions.explanation: Insulin promotes cellular uptake and storage of glucose, lowering blood sugar levels.

questions.question: What metabolic disease is caused by an inadequate secretion or malfunctioning of insulin by the pancreas?
questions.answer: Diabetes mellitus
questions.explanation: Insufficient insulin results in hyperglycaemia and glucose excretion in urine, diagnosed as diabetes mellitus.

questions.question: Why must insulin prescribed to diabetic patients be administered via subcutaneous injection rather than as an oral pill?
options: Pills taste too bitter to swallow.
Insulin is a protein hormone; if swallowed, gastric pepsin and intestinal proteases would digest it into amino acids before it could be absorbed.
questions.answer: Insulin is a protein hormone; if swallowed, gastric pepsin and intestinal proteases would digest it into amino acids before it could be absorbed.
questions.explanation: Being a polypeptide, oral insulin is degraded by digestive enzymes in the stomach and small intestine.

questions.question: What specialized clusters of endocrine cells inside the human pancreas secrete insulin and glucagon?
questions.answer: Islets of Langerhans
questions.explanation: The Islets of Langerhans are the endocrine micro-organs of the pancreas.

questions.question: How does insulin facilitate the storage of surplus glucose inside the human liver and skeletal muscles?
options: It stimulates the polymerisation of glucose into glycogen (glycogenesis).
It turns glucose into bone calcium.
questions.answer: It stimulates the polymerisation of glucose into glycogen (glycogenesis).
questions.explanation: Insulin activates glycogen synthase to convert circulating glucose into storage glycogen.

title: Gonadal Hormones (Testosterone, Oestrogen) & Feedback Mechanisms
tagline: Pubertal maturation and the homeostatic negative feedback loops governing endocrine secretion.
theoryHtml:
1. Gonadal Hormones at Puberty:

During puberty (adolescence), the brain's pituitary gland secretes gonadotropins that stimulate the primary reproductive organs (gonads) to produce sex hormones:

  • Testes in Males — Testosterone:
    • Secreted by the Leydig cells of the testes.
    • Stimulates the formation of sperm (spermatogenesis).
    • Regulates the development of male secondary sexual characteristics: deepening of the voice, growth of facial, pubic, and body hair, broadening of shoulders, and increased muscle mass.
  • Ovaries in Females — Oestrogen and Progesterone:
    • Oestrogen: Stimulates egg maturation and regulates female secondary sexual characteristics (development of mammary glands/breasts, feminine fat deposition on hips, widening of pelvis).
    • Progesterone: Regulates the thickening of the uterine endometrium, controls the menstrual cycle, and maintains pregnancy.

2. The Feedback Mechanism of Hormone Regulation:

Hormones must be released in precise quantities at exact times. Excess or deficiency leads to severe pathology. How does the body regulate this timing and amount? Through Negative Feedback Mechanisms:

Example — Blood Sugar Feedback Control:

  1. After a meal rich in carbohydrates, glucose is absorbed into the blood, causing blood sugar levels to rise.
  2. This elevated glucose concentration is detected directly by the beta cells of the pancreas.
  3. In response, the pancreas secretes more insulin into the bloodstream.
  4. Insulin stimulates cells to absorb glucose, and causes the liver to store glucose as glycogen, causing blood sugar levels to fall back to normal.
  5. As blood glucose drops back to normal baseline, the stimulus is removed; the pancreas detects this decline and reduces/shuts off further insulin secretion.

This closed negative feedback loop ensures that hormone levels oscillate within tight, healthy homeostatic boundaries!
pointsToRemember: Testosterone (from testes) regulates sperm production and male secondary sexual characteristics at puberty.
Oestrogen and Progesterone (from ovaries) regulate egg maturation, female secondary sexual traits, and the menstrual cycle.
Negative feedback mechanisms regulate the timing and amount of hormone released (e.g. blood sugar level controls insulin secretion).
keyNotes: Board Highlight: Explain how the timing and amount of hormone release are regulated using the feedback mechanism of insulin as an example.

questions.question: Why do plants wilt and shed leaves during severe prolonged drought?
options: Elevated levels of abscisic acid (ABA) close stomata to conserve water and trigger senescence and leaf abscission
questions.answer: Elevated levels of abscisic acid (ABA) close stomata to conserve water and trigger senescence and leaf abscission
questions.explanation: Water stress synthesizes ABA in roots and leaves, triggering guard cell potassium efflux (stomatal closure) and abscission zone development.

questions.question: What prevents the transmission of electrical nerve impulses from jumping uncontrollably between adjacent parallel axon fibres in a nerve bundle?
options: Insulating fatty myelin sheaths covering the axons
questions.answer: Insulating fatty myelin sheaths covering the axons
questions.explanation: Myelin sheaths produced by Schwann cells/oligodendrocytes provide electrical insulation, preventing cross-talk and enabling saltatory conduction.

questions.question: In the male reproductive system, which hormone is required both for developing secondary sexual traits and for stimulating the production of sperms?
questions.answer: Testosterone
questions.explanation: Testosterone acts locally on testicular seminiferous tubules to stimulate spermatogenesis and systemically to induce male virilization.

questions.question: Which of the following actions is a pure cranial reflex (integrated in the brainstem rather than the spinal cord)?
options: Blinking of eyes when an object approaches, and salivation at the sight of food
Withdrawing hand from a hot kettle
questions.answer: Blinking of eyes when an object approaches, and salivation at the sight of food
questions.explanation: Corneal blink and salivation reflexes are mediated through cranial nerves (trigeminal, facial, glossopharyngeal) via brainstem centres.

questions.question: Why do ripened fruits (like bananas or apples) accelerate the ripening of other unripened fruits kept nearby in the same basket?
options: Ripening fruits release the gaseous phytohormone ethylene, which diffuses through air to stimulate ripening enzymes in adjacent fruits
questions.answer: Ripening fruits release the gaseous phytohormone ethylene, which diffuses through air to stimulate ripening enzymes in adjacent fruits
questions.explanation: Ethylene (C₂H₄) is a volatile gaseous plant hormone that promotes fruit softening, starch conversion to sugars, and chlorophyll breakdown.

questions.question: Which male sex hormone secreted by the testes regulates sperm production and the emergence of secondary sexual traits during puberty?
questions.answer: Testosterone
questions.explanation: Testosterone coordinates male spermatogenesis and secondary sexual traits at puberty.

questions.question: Which female hormone secreted by the ovaries is responsible for regulating breast development and the menstrual cycle?
questions.answer: Oestrogen
questions.explanation: Oestrogen coordinates female pubertal maturation and regulates the menstrual cycle.

questions.question: How does the negative feedback mechanism regulate the secretion of insulin when blood glucose levels fall back to normal?
options: The pancreas secretes ten times more insulin.
As blood glucose levels decline, the stimulus to beta cells ceases, causing the pancreas to reduce and shut off further insulin release.
questions.answer: As blood glucose levels decline, the stimulus to beta cells ceases, causing the pancreas to reduce and shut off further insulin release.
questions.explanation: Negative feedback ensures that once the desired setpoint is reached, hormone production decreases.

questions.question: What would happen if the endocrine feedback mechanism regulating insulin secretion failed completely and insulin continued pumping unabated?
options: Blood glucose would rise to infinity.
Blood glucose would drop precipitously to dangerously low levels (hypoglycaemic shock/coma).
The heart would turn into bone.
questions.answer: Blood glucose would drop precipitously to dangerously low levels (hypoglycaemic shock/coma).
questions.explanation: Uncontrolled insulin secretion removes all glucose from blood, starving brain neurons of fuel.

questions.question: Which pair of organs produce both gamete sex cells and endocrine steroid hormones?
questions.answer: Testes and Ovaries
questions.explanation: The gonads (testes and ovaries) serve dual roles: gamete production and sex hormone secretion.
